data.budget: 20 min, no network, no real tool
data.claim: Yes: status is clean only when the runner ran, the exit code is in clean_codes, and the parser accepted the output with no findings.
data.falsifier: Any scripted runner outcome that is not (ran, clean exit code, parseable, no findings) yet yields status clean.
data.mechanism: TableTool.run returns early with UNAVAILABLE on each failure branch before any CLEAN return; the production runner (cmdrunner) already reports missing/timeout/could-not-run/busy as ran=False.
data.probe: uv run --with pytest-xdist pytest -n 16 -q tests/test_adapter_tools.py tests/test_ports_contract.py
data.probe_output: 65+ passed incl. parametrized missing/timeout/could_not_run/not_found/busy, unexpected exit code, unparseable output, findings-exit-without-findings, unmet pin, raising runner each asserting status unavailable; the same cases pass against FakeExternalTool.
data.question: Can one table-described ExternalTool adapter over an injected runner map every failure mode (missing, timeout, could-not-run, unknown exit code, unparseable output, findings-exit with no findings, unmet pin, raising runner) to unavailable and never to clean?

evidence.note: Research note R55e58fea66 CONFIRMED: every failure mode scripted in tests/test_adapter_tools.py and the shared conformance cases yields unavailable, never clean; pytest tests/test_adapter_tools.py tests/test_ports_contract.py all pass.

Read r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, r-small-files, r-reuse-core, r-everything-configurable: every reason names the next step; timeouts are two companions knobs; files under 20 KB; runs go through cmdrunner, no second runner.
Commits d067c2d41, d154847f9, 762d77c6a on ddflow/ADP-tools; tests/test_adapter_tools.py 45+ tests, port/fake/conformance in the modular layout; ruff clean.

data.command: [REDACTED:path] -m ddflow --agent adp-tools review ADP-tools --gate rubber_duck,critic --branch ddflow/ADP-tools

chunk_findings.detail: `scripted` is documented as returning “a copy of this fake,” but it does not preserve the existing scripted `probe`/`run` when only one of them is supplied. For example, given `FakeExternalTool(probe=RunResult(False, kind=MISSING))`, calling `.scripted(run=RunResult(True, 0, "[]"))` creates a new fake whose `probe` argument is `None`, so `__init__` replaces the missing-tool probe with the default successful probe. The resulting fake then answers `.probe()` as installed with version `1.0.0`, even though the original fake was configured to simulate a missing tool. This can silently make tests or conformance cases pass when they should see the original unavailable probe.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/tools.py:scripted

chunk_findings.detail: `_json_list` raises `ToolParseError` with the first 80 characters of the raw tool output, and `parse_gitleaks` raises with the first 80 characters of a report row. For gitleaks output, this copies secrets into the exception message. For example, `parse_gitleaks("gitleaks", "Secret: [REDACTED] raises a `ToolParseError` containing `Secret: [REDACTED] and `parse_gitleaks("gitleaks", '[{"Secret":"hunter2"}]')` raises a `ToolParseError` containing the row with the secret. The module contract explicitly says a parser never copies a secret; these failure paths violate that and can leak secrets into unavailable reasons or logs.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tool_parsers.py:_json_list

chunk_findings.detail: JSON `null` in optional normalized fields becomes the literal string `"None"` instead of being treated as absent/empty. For input `[{"rule":"r","severity":null,"file":null,"advisory":null}]`, `parse_normalized` returns a `Finding` with `severity="None"`, `file="None"`, and `advisory="None"`. The same issue exists in `parse_gitleaks` for `File: null`. That is wrong because JSON null means the field is not present/has no value, not that the field’s value is the string `"None"`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tool_parsers.py:parse_normalized

chunk_findings.detail:
`parse_precommit` scans every output line after `line.strip()`, so any indented hook output or diff line that happens to match the hook-status pattern becomes a false finding. For pre-commit output such as:

```text
mypy....Failed
  test_foo....Failed
```

or a diff line `+test....Failed`, the parser returns extra findings for `test_foo` or `+test`, even though those are not top-level pre-commit hook result lines. This produces incorrect normalized findings from arbitrary hook output or diffs.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tool_parsers.py:parse_precommit

chunk_findings.detail: `ToolProbe.usable` treats an unknown pin result as usable. For `ToolProbe(tool="semgrep", installed=True, pin="1.70.0", pinned_ok=None)`, `usable` returns `True` because the code only rejects `pinned_ok is False`. But `pinned_ok` is documented as `None` both when there is no pin and when a pin is set but no version could be read; in the latter case the required pin is not known to be satisfied, so the probe should not be usable. A caller that uses `usable` to decide whether a scanner may run or is available would accept a scanner with an unverified required version, contrary to the intent that probing checks whether the pinned version is satisfied and that “not knowing is not usable.”
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tool_types.py:97

chunk_findings.detail: `spec_from_row()` documents that a row that cannot work is refused when read, but it does not validate `version_re` as a regex. A `[[tool]]` row with `version_re = "("` passes row validation, and then `TableTool.probe()` raises `re.error` at `re.search(s.version_re, ...)`. A related valid-regex case is `version_re = r"(\d+)?"` with version output containing no digits: `re.search` returns a match whose first group is `None`, so the expression `m.group(1) ... .strip()` raises `AttributeError`. In both cases a gate crashes instead of receiving an unavailable probe, contrary to the port’s “every failure maps to unavailable” rule.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tools.py:TableTool.probe

chunk_findings.detail: `run()` only catches `ToolParseError` around parsing, but the stated contract is that every failure is mapped to an unavailable `ToolRun`. If `self.parse()` raises any other exception, `run()` propagates it. For example, if a registered spec has a parser name not present in `PARSERS` (possible by bypassing `spec_from_row` validation, e.g. via direct `TableTool` construction or `SPECS.register` if registration does not revalidate), `PARSERS[self.spec.parser]` raises `KeyError` inside `run()` instead of returning a `ToolRun` with status `unavailable`. The same applies to a parser that raises `ValueError`/`TypeError` on unexpected output rather than `ToolParseError`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tools.py:TableTool.run

chunk_findings.detail: `command_tool_runner` selects the runner with `runner or CommandRunner()` instead of `runner is None`. If a caller passes a valid runner object that happens to be falsy (for example a fake command runner with `__bool__` returning `False`, or a sequence-like fake with no queued commands), the `or` expression treats it as absent and constructs a real `CommandRunner`. In that case `call` will execute real subprocesses instead of using the injected fake, so a test or caller that deliberately supplies a falsy runner gets real tool execution/consent behavior rather than the injected fake, violating the injection contract and the conformance requirement that fakes replace subprocesses.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/toolrun.py:31

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds a new kept entry, `"ddflow/services/toolrun.py:external_tool" = "SEC-scanners"`, growing an existing guard baseline. The stated conformance for this change says “baselines only shrink,” so introducing a new unreferenced-function exception is a defect: if `SEC-scanners` is not yet present or does not actually call `external_tool`, the guard now hides dead/unwired code that previously would have been reported.
chunk_findings.title: tests/guard_baselines/unreferenced_functions.toml:17

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to verify that `cwd` is passed, but it cannot detect a missing `cwd`: `Script.calls` records only `(list(argv), timeout_s)`, and the assertions check only argv and timeout. If `TableTool.run` is implemented as `runner(argv, timeout_s=timeout_s, cwd=None)` while ignoring the caller-supplied `cwd="/w"`, this test still passes. The input is a run call with `cwd="/w"`; the expected failure is that the command runner receives `/w`, but the test does not inspect the third argument.
chunk_findings.title: `test_run_appends_args_and_passes_the_timeout_and_cwd`

chunk_findings.detail: These production-runner tests hard-code the interpreter name `python3`. On a valid environment where the test interpreter is available only as `python` or via `sys.executable` but not as `python3` on `PATH` (e.g., many Windows setups or some virtualenvs), `command_tool_runner(["python3", "-c", "print('hi')"], timeout_s=20)` returns `ran=False` with kind `MISSING`, so the test fails even though the production runner is correct for the actual interpreter. The test should use `sys.executable` instead of `python3`.
chunk_findings.title: `test_the_production_runner_maps_missing_and_timeout_and_runs_a_real_argv`
ddflow/adapters/tool_parsers.py:39

chunk_findings.detail: The property returns `installed is True and pinned_ok is not False`, so `pinned_ok=None` is treated as usable. But `ToolProbe` documents that `pinned_ok` is `None` either when no pin is set or when no version could be read, and `usable`'s own docstring says "Not knowing is not usable." Given `ToolProbe(tool="gitleaks", installed=True, version="", pin=">=8.0", pinned_ok=None, reason="version probe timed out")`, `usable` is `True`; a caller can treat an unverified version as satisfying the pin and run/pass the tool.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tool_types.py:ToolProbe.usable

chunk_findings.detail: `spec_from_row` claims a row that cannot work is refused when it is read, but it never validates `version_re`. A `[[tool]]` row with an invalid regular expression such as `version_re = "("` is accepted by `SPECS`; the first `probe()` then reaches `re.search(s.version_re, ...)` and raises `re.error` instead of returning a `ToolProbe`. That is a crash in the port’s own probe method rather than the promised `unavailable`/could-not-tell result (`ExternalTool` port contract: a failure is never passed; probe failures should be normalized, not raised).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tools.py:spec_from_row

chunk_findings.detail: The relative link `[README.md](README.md)` resolves from `docs/ddflow/adapters/` to `docs/ddflow/adapters/README.md`, but the change’s manifest lists only the root `README.md` (the generated/pinned file excluded from review), not a `docs/ddflow/adapters/README.md`. Rendering this page therefore produces a broken link; it should point to `../../../README.md` or use a root-relative path.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/adapters/tools.md:22

chunk_findings.detail: In the conformance test suite (`CONFORMANCE` dictionary on lines 320-332), the `CONFORMANCE` structure defines `"real"` as a lambda taking `monkeypatch` and returning `_Kit()`, but the test runner or framework is expected to iterate over `CONFORMANCE` and run `cases(kit)` or similar. However, `test_the_default_adapter_passes_the_tool_cases` and `test_the_fake_passes_the_tool_cases` bypass `CONFORMANCE` entirely by calling `tool_cases(_Kit())` and `tool_cases(FakeExternalTool(...))` directly, leaving the defined `CONFORMANCE` dictionary completely unused and dead code, violating the explicit intent that a conformance test runs the same cases against the adapter and the fake via the conformance runner.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_adapter_tools.py:326

data.command: [REDACTED:path] -m ddflow --agent adp-tools review ADP-tools --gate rubber_duck,critic --branch ddflow/ADP-tools --intent 'ExternalTool port; prior round findings fixed: no echoed output, pin unknown not usable, version_re validated, null fields, indent, falsy runner'

chunk_findings.detail: `scripted` documents itself as returning “a copy of this fake,” but it does not copy the fake’s existing scripted `probe`/`run` results: omitted arguments are passed as `None` and then replaced by the constructor’s default successful `RunResult`s. For example, `missing = FakeExternalTool(probe=RunResult(False, kind=MISSING, reason="missing"))`; `copy = missing.scripted(run=RunResult(True, 0, "[]"))`; then `copy.probe().installed` returns `True`, not `False`. A test or conformance case that scripts only one operation on a base fake will silently get a different probe/run result, potentially hiding an unavailable/missing-tool condition.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/tools.py:scripted

chunk_findings.detail:
`_HOOK_LINE` is matched against every stripped line of the whole `pre-commit` output, including hook stdout/stderr. Given output where a hook’s own output contains a line that looks like a status line, e.g.
```
check yaml...............................................................Failed
some test...Failed
```
`parse_precommit` returns two findings, one with rule `some test`. That second line is not a pre-commit hook summary line, so the parser can invent findings from arbitrary tool output.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tool_parsers.py:98

chunk_findings.detail:
The regex allows an optional parenthetical only before the state and then anchors the state at end-of-line. Pre-commit can emit a parenthetical reason after the state, e.g.
```
check json...............................................................Failed (files were modified by this hook)
```
This line does not match `_HOOK_LINE`, so `parse_precommit` returns no finding for that failed hook.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tool_parsers.py:98

chunk_findings.detail: `ToolProbe.usable` returns `True` when `installed is True` and `pinned_ok is None`, but `pinned_ok` is documented as `None` both when no pin is set and when the pinned version could not be read. For `ToolProbe(tool="semgrep", installed=True, pin="1.60.0", pinned_ok=None)`, `usable` returns `True`, so a caller can treat the tool as usable even though the required version was not verified. That contradicts the docstring (“Not knowing is not usable”) and the port intent that probe must establish that the pinned version is satisfied and that unavailable/unknown is never treated as passed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tool_types.py:97

chunk_findings.detail: `probe` assumes that if the configured `version_re` has any capture group, group 1 participated and is a string. A valid regex with an optional first capture group makes `m.groups()` non-empty while `m.group(1)` is `None`, so the following `.strip()` raises `AttributeError` instead of returning a three-valued/unavailable probe. For example, a row with `version_re = r"v?(\d+\.\d+)?"` and a version command that exits 0 with stdout `v` matches, `m.groups()` is `(None,)`, and `version = (m.group(1) if m and m.groups() else m.group(0) if m else "").strip()` crashes on `None.strip()`. That is a failure path in the adapter, but the port’s stated rule is that probe/run failures become `unavailable`/could-not-tell, not an exception.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tools.py:TableTool.probe

chunk_findings.detail: The ExternalTool port is a new adapter family, but its `tool_probe_timeout_s` and `tool_run_timeout_s` knobs are added to the existing shared `companions` config section instead of a file owned by the new port. This violates the project guidance that “a new port touches only its own files” [r-adapters]: a second change adding a companion knob will collide in this file, and ExternalTool timeout configuration is coupled to the unrelated companion section rather than the port’s own configuration surface.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/companions.py:21

chunk_findings.detail: The diff adds a new `[kept]` baseline entry for `ddflow/services/toolrun.py:external_tool`, which grows the unreferenced-function baseline. The change’s conformance requirement says “baselines only shrink,” so this addition is the opposite. The manifest shows no SEC-scanners caller in the 12-file change, so the new production wiring is currently unreferenced and the baseline entry suppresses that fact instead of either adding the caller or omitting the unreferenced function.
chunk_findings.title: tests/guard_baselines/unreferenced_functions.toml:17

chunk_findings.detail: The bad-import predicate exempts three-dot relative imports: `i.startswith("..") and not i.startswith("...")`. For a module in `ddflow/adapters/tools.py`, `_imports` turns `from ... import subprocess` into `"...subprocess"` (or `from ... import os` into `"..."`); that string does not start with `subprocess`/`os`, and the `not startswith("...")` clause explicitly excludes it from `bad`. The test therefore passes even though the import is above the adapters package and can start a process, so the layering guard has a false negative [r-adapters].
chunk_findings.title: `test_tool_modules_import_nothing_above_adapters_and_start_no_process`

chunk_findings.detail: The test calls `run(..., cwd="/w")`, but `Script.__call__` records only `(list(argv), timeout_s)` and the test never inspects `cwd`. If `TableTool.run` ignores the `cwd` argument and calls the runner with `cwd=None`, the argv and timeout assertions still pass. The test therefore does not verify the advertised contract that `run` forwards `cwd`; a tool run in the wrong directory would not be caught.
chunk_findings.title: `test_run_appends_args_and_passes_the_timeout_and_cwd`

chunk_findings.detail: When no JSON array is found, `_json_list` embeds the first 80 characters of raw output in the `ToolParseError` message. This contradicts the module’s own guarantee that a parser never copies a secret. For example, if a wrapper using `parse_normalized` emits output such as `{"secret": "sk-live-1234567890"}` instead of a JSON array, the error string contains the secret and `ExternalTool.run` is intended to carry that exception into the `unavailable` result, so the secret can be logged or persisted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tool_parsers.py:48 _json_list

chunk_findings.detail: `_json_list` returns the first valid JSON array anywhere in the output, not necessarily the report array after leading log lines. A tool or wrapper that logs a JSON-array line before its actual finding array triggers a parse error. Given `parse_normalized("fake", '["starting scan"]\n[{"rule":"r1","severity":"high","file":"a","line":1}]')`, `_json_list` returns `["starting scan"]`; `parse_normalized` then sees a string row and raises `ToolParseError`, although a valid report follows. `ExternalTool.run` converts that parse error into `unavailable` instead of the finding, defeating the function’s stated purpose of allowing log lines before a report.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tool_parsers.py:46 _json_list

chunk_findings.detail: `usable` returns `self.installed is True and self.pinned_ok is not False`, so `pinned_ok=None` is treated as usable. But `ToolProbe` documents that `pinned_ok` is `None` when “no pin is set or no version could be read,” and `usable`’s own docstring says “Not knowing is not usable.” Concrete input: `ToolProbe(tool="gitleaks", installed=True, pin=">=8.0.0", version="", pinned_ok=None)` (version probe failed or timed out) makes `usable` return `True`, allowing a caller to run a tool whose required minimum version was never verified, contrary to the adapter contract that unknown is unavailable and never clean.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tool_types.py:92 (`ToolProbe.usable`)

chunk_findings.detail: `spec_from_row` accepts any `version_re` string without compiling/validating it, and `probe()` calls `re.search(s.version_re, ...)` outside the `try` in `_call`. A malformed regex in `tools.toml` (for example `version_re = "("`) makes `probe()` raise `re.error` instead of returning a `ToolProbe`/`unavailable`. This violates the adapter’s stated contract that every failure maps to `unavailable` and the `spec_from_row` docstring that a bad row is refused when read, not when a gate reaches for it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tools.py:probe

chunk_findings.detail: `_version_key` treats every run of digits as a numeric version component. `version_at_least("8.30.0-rc.1", "8.30.0")` compares `(8,30,0,1)` >= `(8,30,0,0)` and returns `True`, so a pre-release satisfies a stable pin; conversely a release is reported as not satisfying a pre-release pin even though the release is newer. With a `version_re` that captures the full version string, this can let an unpinned pre-release pass a gate that requires a stable version.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tools.py:version_at_least

chunk_findings.detail: The file declares only four `[[tool]]` entries: roborev, gitleaks, pre-commit, and prek. The change intent says the ExternalTool port is for pip-audit, osv-scanner, and semgrep as well, and this is the data file that `ddflow.adapters.tools` uses to turn rows into `ExternalTool`s. With no entries for pip-audit, osv-scanner, or semgrep, a caller asking for `tool_id="semgrep"` (for example) cannot resolve an adapter, so those required tools are absent from the implementation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/tools.toml

chunk_findings.detail: `command_tool_runner` defaults the runner with `runner or CommandRunner()` rather than `runner if runner is not None else CommandRunner()`, relying on truthiness instead of presence. Given a `CommandRunner` instance whose `__bool__`/`__len__` returns `False` (for example a `CommandRunner` subclass used as a no-op in a test harness), the supplied runner is silently discarded and a real `CommandRunner` is used instead. This violates the parameter contract “use the provided runner when one is provided” and can cause real subprocess execution where the caller intended no subprocess.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/toolrun.py:23

chunk_findings.detail: The diff adds a new `[kept]` entry for `ddflow/services/toolrun.py:external_tool`, growing the unreferenced-functions baseline by one. The change's own stated conformance criterion is “baselines only shrink”; adding a new kept suppression is a growth of the baseline, so this line violates that criterion and prevents the guard from reporting `external_tool` as unreferenced if it is not actually statically reachable.
chunk_findings.title: tests/guard_baselines/unreferenced_functions.toml:17

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named and documented as checking that `cwd` is passed to the runner, but `Script.__call__` accepts `cwd` and does not record or assert it. The assertion only inspects `argv` and `timeout_s`, so an implementation that silently drops `cwd` still passes. This is a false-positive test: call `T.tool("gitleaks", sc, run_timeout_s=11).run(["--source", "x"], cwd="/w")` and `run` ignores `cwd`; the test still passes.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_adapter_tools.py:test_run_appends_args_and_passes_the_timeout_and_cwd

chunk_findings.detail: The test invokes `python3` directly and also uses it in `test_an_argument_with_shell_syntax_stays_one_argv_token`. On systems where the interpreter is only available as `python` or `py` (Windows, many CI images), the executable is not found and the test fails before exercising the runner. The suite should use `sys.executable`; the docstring claim that `python3` is “always present” is not true.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_adapter_tools.py:test_the_production_runner_maps_missing_and_timeout_and_runs_a_real_argv

chunk_findings.detail: `command_tool_runner` is the default implementation for subprocess tool execution, so [r-adapters] requires it to live in `ddflow/adapters` next to the `ExternalTool` port. The manifest puts it in `ddflow/services/toolrun.py`, and this part’s tests import it from `ddflow.services.toolrun`, so the external-dependency implementation escapes the adapter boundary rather than touching only its adapter files.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/toolrun.py:command_tool_runner

chunk_findings.detail: The regex `re.search(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)+", p.out + p.err)` used to extract the tool version in `FakeExternalTool.probe` can concatenate `p.out` and `p.err` without a separator. If the last character of `p.out` and the first character of `p.err` are both digits, they will be incorrectly joined into a single larger version number (e.g., `out="v1.2"` and `err="3"` becomes `"1.23"` instead of `"1.2.3"`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/adapters/fakes/tools.py:72
